videos.title: simon gale   power of community   insights into the usta national campus v1 (1080p)

segments.description: Coaches, our next presenter is Simon Gale, the Senior Director of Racket Sports Development at the USTA National Campus. Simon leads a team managing over 100 courts and hundreds of programs annually. An award-winning industry leader, Simon specializes in Racket Sports Innovation and Operational Excellence. His session, Racket Sports Leadership and Program Excellence will provide insights into successful and impactful programs, in particular how he has integrated complementary formats into his program at the USTA. Welcome Simon. Welcome to the USTA National Campus. My name is Simon Gale and the title of my presentation is The Power of Community. My goal is to show you how by engaging in your community you can build a thriving Racket Sports program to include tennis, pickleball, puddle or other complementary Racket Sports. I've been in the States for over 25 years, moving from Perth, Australia originally. I've held titles as Director of Tennis, Director of Racket Sports, General Manager and also an owner and managing partner at a facility. When I came to the campus I came as the Director of Tennis and I currently hold the role of Senior Director of Racket Sports Development here at the USTA. Let me tell you a little bit about the USTA National Campus. We opened in January 2017 and currently have 100 courts including tennis, pickleball and puddle. We have 35 teaching pros that deliver 135 programs per week with over 2000 guests who

come and participate in those programs. We also host over 350 events per year with a total of more than 300,000 annual visitors making the National Campus an incredibly busy facility. We are also the home of prestigious USTA National Championships and annual events as well as the NCAA Championships, Billie Jean King Cup and recently have hosted professional pickleball association tour events. From the start we've been known as the home of American Tennis yet in June 2020 we embarked on a major renovation project to become a community hub for racket sports. As a result our connection with the community has increased tremendously. So how did we get started? We added four permanent pickleball courts, four new puddle courts as well as adding blended lines to our existing junior tennis courts. But if you look where I am now I'm on a tennis court, full-sized tennis court and we've got four blended line courts that are taped down here and for many of you that's where you have to start. Five, six years ago when I first started at my own facility this is what it looked like. We tested it and once we saw that there was a proven concept we then painted lines on our tennis courts and that's how we started before we evolved into building purpose-built pickleball courts. When complementary racket sports first hit the market here in the States there was a lot of resistance from tennis coaches and tennis facilities.

It probably takes you about 20 minutes to set up a court and then use it as a trial. If it works then you can look at the continued investment into whether you have more permanent facilities. Four new Padel courts which have proved to be incredibly popular. We've seen a tremendous amount of tennis players transition from tennis to Padel. Let's talk about me for a minute. When I first got here five years ago my role was director of tennis and now with the addition of Padel and pickleball it's changed the director of racket sports which I'm okay with. my role tremendously and so now I've had to oversee three sports and learn the nuances in the business model of these two new sports as well. So we were trying to build a new identity that would make us a national model for racket's program and from this vantage point you can see all three racket sports that we offer tennis, pickleball as well as Padel and at the core of all of this tennis remains and tennis has grown three to four times over the last four years and we have an incredibly healthy program nothing has suffered as a result of adding complementary racket sports to our programming offers. So while we were fully embracing this concept universally throughout the country the concept of the national campus becoming a racket sports facility was not necessarily adopted by all it's still to this day is controversial with some who think we should just be promoting tennis. Now while tennis is our primary push and always will be these complementary racket sports have added to the experience here at the campus and I've talked about how it attracted an entirely new clientele but for the average day facility owner they're trying to maximize square footage they're looking at ways to engage their members keep their members from going down the road to play somewhere and how do we add value to their experience. So you are seeing this across the country and it's being adopted by a lot of facilities

who have now added pickleball or Padel and in the northeast we're seeing platform tennis as well. So this is something that is happening and it's important that the campus reflects this and is able to talk to the business model. So it's been invaluable for me to be able to talk to other directors throughout the country about how we started the evolution and where we are today and they're able to take some of those best practices and apply them to their own businesses. So our goal was to build a new identity as a racket sports program to become more diverse and engage with our community. We aim to be known as versatile innovative and progressive with how we deliver a healthy racket's program to our local people. The other thing that was very important was to make sure our pros were educated so we invested in education and had them all trained and explained the business model and where we were headed with this and we only wanted pros who were engaged and wanted to be part of this we would never force them to have to come and teach an additional sport but for those who wanted to diversify it was a great opportunity for them. As a result we've gone from having one part-time pro to now having a head professional full time another full-time teaching professional as well as multiple part-time pros who teach tennis and pickleball. So the reality of our situation was that we needed to adjust.

We planned around a 70% play program and 30% where we would have pros involved. We're not getting the foot traffic and needed to pivot quickly. As a result we came up with something called community drop-in and the basis of that was how do we engage with our community and get new people to come and play at the campus. We needed foot traffic because we had our identity issue. We were a tennis facility dabbling in pickleball. So by adding pickleball we needed to connect with the community and did so through adding this new free community drop-in. The basic premise of that was we created three sessions per week for an hour and a half and we would take up to 40 players on eight of our racket sports courts. I had one pro who we didn't want a teaching pro. We wanted someone who could facilitate play. We didn't want a traditional lesson type program. We wanted people to come and play because the sport is a playing sport and as a result of that we exceeded expectations and were able to put in a play facilitator who then helped push these people into our existing programs and as a result our program took off. So what I want to do is make sure it's clear what a play facilitator is versus having a coach on the court. The play facilitator's role is to just do that, facilitate play. So we did a training session with our team on what that looked like. Instead of having a basket on a court and a pro feeding and correcting technique, we

wanted somebody to manage a large group over eight courts so we had 40 people on eight courts which makes it very difficult for that pro to impart technical adjustments. Their job was to get people playing as quickly as possible and it doesn't matter how good it looks. The goal is to get people playing. The benefit to this pro is that they're then able to be put in front of 40 people who then they can facilitate getting lessons from, whether that's privates or upselling them to move into our programs and if that pro is connected to pickleball then they're also going to be teaching these people in the future as well. So this was a win-win for our pros as well as for our program because it keeps our cost way down for the delivery of this program. One of the beauties of using one of our teaching professionals was the ability to keep our cost down from a marketing point of view. A pro or facilitator cost me $10,000 for 12 months for three times per week. We injected no additional money into marketing other than Facebook and word of mouth. So it was very affordable and we had a huge return by the end of the year on this program. So since opening in June 2020 we're only four years in so we're very young as a pickleball program but we've had tremendous growth and success to a point where we're now hosting nationally recognized camps, major professional events and a thriving community program.

And our numbers for our community drop in reflect that success. So some of the key outcomes, we've been able to build a thriving rackets community. It's a truly inclusive space where we've engaged with people who said to us, we're never coming. We know you're there but we're never going to come and play tennis, it's too difficult but we think we can play one of those sports. So as a result we've been able to feed them into the community and be part of our rackets program and then what we hope is that some of them will try tennis or their kids or grandkids will come and try tennis and as a result we've created a healthier playing community. Part of our mission is to create healthier communities and so this fulfills our mission. The other thing that's happened is we've been able to certify all of our pros in pickleball and those who were passionate about it have been injected into the program delivery. Additionally those who were interested in PDEL and being part of our PDEL program were also able to get certified in PDEL. As a result we've created new diverse income streams for those pros and we've created an opportunity for them that one day when they leave the campus they'll be employable as director of racket sports in the future. With more people coming through the building our pro shop has benefited as a result. We've had to add pickleball and PDEL equipment and with all these people playing with these

new sports they've seen an uptick in sales. So what's new in our pro shop what used to just be tennis is now PDEL and we've also had to add pickleball frames and paddles so that our customers have a full service pro shop and as you can hear our food and beverage sales have increased as a result of more people coming to participate in these racket sports. So here are the results of our community drop-in pickleball program. We see around 600 total players per month representing 800 unique players over the course of a year. We've been able to convert 60% of those free customers into paying customers which is injected around $150,000 of new revenue. Our sources of revenue include programming, tournaments, lessons, private lessons and events and one of the unexpected revenue sources has been increased court time. So despite these people coming for free and looking for free court time outside the campus they've now developed a community of players who now engage and play at the campus and pay for court timing. Complementary racket sports now make up around 15% of our annual revenue and what's been very interesting to see is tennis is about 95% pro-based programming and 5% without a pro or play-based and pickleball represents around 82% with pro and 18% play. So very similar models despite the general message that pickleball is a playing sport and they do not take lessons. So one of the most important key takeaways was that we needed to offer this for free.

We are competing with free courts at public parks and homeowners associations and as a result we weren't getting the foot traffic. As soon as we went to free the traffic obviously increased dramatically. So it's very important that we offered a free product and from there fed our programs. The other thing that was really important that we learned quickly was the importance having a full pathway for these people to experience. So once they came and tried and decided they wanted to get better we needed to have complementary programming where they could move in and take 101 classes or advanced classes or move into tournaments and be able to complete a full pathway of events. The other thing that was critical was the play facilitator which I've talked about before. However the right person was critical. We didn't want to coach. You have to have somebody who's there to just high five people maybe give a turbo tip from time to time but it's all about play and enthusiasm and upselling our programs. So part of our strategic plan is to make better data driven decisions moving forward. What we wanted to also do was get these play facilitators to buy into the data. Many opposed the free concept but when you present that as a result of free we added X number of clinics and injected $150,000 of new income then they were sold and became more invested in the product. So we've just completed a major renovation of our family zone area to now include 14

racket sports courts which will host Red Bull for adults, Red Bull for juniors as well as pickleball programming. Our goal in this space is to have 75 to 80 percent occupancy and between all three sports we're comfortable and confident that that's something we can achieve. We're also looking to expand our pickleball program by adding a comprehensive junior pathway. So what's next? Due to the success of our community drop-in pickleball program we're looking to replicate that and create a community drop-in Red Bull for adult tennis program. So what we will be offering is three one-and-a-half hour sessions per week with 40 players. Our goal is to have up to 500 players per month come and visit the campus and by years in we're hoping to have 800 unique players come through the facility and try tennis. One of the critical success factors for this program is making sure we do not have a coach run this we are looking for a play facilitator who can get people playing tennis as quick as possible. Our goal will be to convert 60 percent of those into paying customers which will generate an additional revenue total of around $150,000 per year. Our journey to become a racquet sports community is a reflection of what's happening across the country here in the U.S. I know in Australia you're just getting started with these complementary racquet sports specifically pickleball, padel and even pop tennis.

However, the evolution into becoming a director of racquet sports is very real here and I think it's coming your way in Australia as well. Players are looking to maximize square footage and make the most engaging experience for members and guests as possible. So get ahead of this, develop your team, become subject matter experts in these complementary racquet sports and look for opportunities to insert programming that both engages your community but engages your members and will give you real job security moving forward. Thank you for listening to my presentation.
